content.content: {"result":"{\"success\": true, \"data\": {\"stdout\": \"# Discussion (Draft)\\n\\n## Training-time vs Inference-time Structural Information\\n\\nA growing body of work integrates structural code information into retrieval and localization systems, but the *stage* at which structural information is consumed differs fundamentally across methods. CodexGraph (Liu et al., NAACL 2025) materializes a code property graph in a Neo4j database and exposes a Cypher query interface that an LLM agent invokes at inference time; each query triggers multiple rounds of LLM-guided graph traversal, incurring latency proportional to task complexity. LocAgent (Chen et al., ACL 2025) similarly constructs a directed heterogeneous graph with call, import, and inheritance edges, achieving 92.7% file-level localization on SWE-bench-Lite—but again through multi-turn LLM inference over the graph at query time. RANGER (Shah et al., 2025) and RepoGraph (Ouyang et al., ICLR 2025) follow the same paradigm: runtime graph construction and traversal with per-query computational cost that scales linearly with query volume. [源: plan_017]\\n\\nStructFuse takes a different approach by amortizing all structural computation into the training phase. We perform bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis (2-hop call-graph scope) via CodeQL as a one-time extraction step—approximately 8.9 seconds per instance, totaling ~110 hours for 44K instances with zero timeouts—and use the resulting connectivity information exclusively for hard negative mining during contrastive training. At inference time, the trained encoder operates at standard embedding speed with no graph overhead. This design makes StructFuse suited for latency-sensitive, high-throughput retrieval scenarios where per-query graph traversal would be prohibitive. [源: m1_extraction / plan_006]\\n\\nThe two paradigms are complementary rather than competing. A StructFuse-trained encoder, whose representations already encode data-flow semantics, can serve as a first-stage retriever that narrows the candidate set before an inference-time graph agent (e.g., LocAgent or CodexGraph) performs targeted structural reranking. Evaluating such hybrid pipelines is a natural direction for future work. We note that direct numerical comparison between StructFuse and inference-time graph methods is methodologically challenging: they address different task interfaces (embedding-based ranked retrieval vs. multi-turn agentic localization) and have been evaluated on different benchmarks under different metrics. [源: plan_017]\\n\\n## Inter-procedural vs Intra-procedural Scope\\n\\nAmong methods that incorporate data-flow or control-flow analysis, scope varies considerably. GraphCoder (Liu et al., ASE 2024) constructs a Code Context Graph combining control-flow, control-dependence, and data-dependence subgraphs—the closest to StructFuse in leveraging data-flow semantics—but its analysis is strictly intra-procedural: no information crosses function boundaries. ARISE (Seddik & Fard, 2026) performs repository-level graph construction with data-flow edges, yet its data-flow analysis is also intra-procedural, limited to within-function def-use chains, with cross-function relationships captured only through structural edges (call, inheritance). CodexGraph and LocAgent capture call graphs and inheritance hierarchies but model no data-flow semantics at all—edges represent syntactic relationships (who calls whom), not how values propagate. [源: plan_017]\\n\\nStructFuse occupies a middle ground: bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis with a 2-hop call-graph scope. This design crosses function boundaries to capture indirect data dependencies (e.g., a value defined in function A that flows through function B to affect function C) while remaining computationally tractable. Our plan_006 analysis shows that 2-hop scoping covers Z=40.8% of query-candidate pairs with structural connectivity, with median coverage reaching 96% for extra-large repositories where inter-procedural dependencies are most prevalent. The bounding trades completeness for scalability: deeper call chains (>2 hops) are truncated, but the resulting extraction completes with 0% timeout rate across 123 repositories. Exploring larger hop bounds (3-hop and beyond) via plan_007 ablation remains a direction for future investigation. [源: plan_006 / m1_extraction]\\n\\n## Limitations\\n\\n**Bounded inter-procedural scope.** The 2-hop call-graph bounding in our CodeQL extraction truncates data-flow paths that traverse more than two function boundaries. While 2-hop coverage reaches Z=40.8% overall and is high for large repositories (median 96% for XL repos), deep call chains characteristic of certain architectural patterns (e.g., deeply layered middleware stacks, recursive visitor patterns) may be incompletely captured. The planned hop-count ablation (plan_007) will quantify the marginal value of extending the analysis boundary, though we expect diminishing returns as longer paths introduce noise from increasingly indirect dependencies. [���: plan_006]\\n\\n**Language and tooling constraints.** Our structural extraction relies on CodeQL, which supports a fixed set of languages (Python, Java, JavaScript, C/C++, Go, Ruby, C#, Swift). For languages outside this set, alternative static analysis frameworks (e.g., tree-sitter for syntax, Joern for data-flow) would be required, and the quality of bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis may differ. The method's core principle—using structural connectivity for training-time negative mining—is language-agnostic, but the specific extraction pipeline is not. [源: m1_extraction]\\n\\n**Structural data coverage.** In the current M1 extraction, 36% of instances yield structural data, meaning 64% lack data-flow connectivity information and fall back to non-structural negative mining strategies. This rate reflects runtime extraction failures rather than a fundamental limitation of the approach; a planned re-extraction (m1_reextract_v2) with improved error handling is expected to raise coverage substantially. Nonetheless, even at full coverage, instances from small or self-contained repositories may genuinely lack inter-procedural data-flow paths, limiting the applicability of structure-grounded negatives for those cases. [源: m1_extraction / registry]\\n\\n**Statistical power.** Our current results are based on n=3 random seeds per configuration, yielding df=2 for pairwise comparisons. This limits statistical power and increases Type II error risk—observed effect sizes (+1.6–2.0pp R@1 for embedding mining, +0.8–2.3pp for dataflow negatives on Qwen) may not reach conventional significance thresholds. The full M2 experimental matrix (9 seeds × 3 strategies × 2 encoders) is in progress and will provide adequate power for bootstrap confidence interval estimation. Until then, we characterize our findings as observed patterns with mechanistic support rather than statistically confirmed effects. [源: m2_full / plan_016]\\n\", \"stderr\": \"\", \"return_code\": 0}, \"error\": null, \"metadata\": {\"elapsed_seconds\": 0.35}}"}

## Training-time vs Inference-time Structural Information

A growing body of work integrates structural code information into retrieval and localization systems, but the *stage* at which structural information is consumed differs fundamentally across methods. CodexGraph (Liu et al., NAACL 2025) materializes a code property graph in a Neo4j database and exposes a Cypher query interface that an LLM agent invokes at inference time; each query triggers multiple rounds of LLM-guided graph traversal, incurring latency proportional to task complexity. LocAgent (Chen et al., ACL 2025) similarly constructs a directed heterogeneous graph with call, import, and inheritance edges, achieving 92.7% file-level localization on SWE-bench-Lite—but again through multi-turn LLM inference over the graph at query time. RANGER (Shah et al., 2025) and RepoGraph (Ouyang et al., ICLR 2025) follow the same paradigm: runtime graph construction and traversal with per-query computational cost that scales linearly with query volume. [源: plan_017]

StructFuse takes a different approach by amortizing all structural computation into the training phase. We perform bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis (2-hop call-graph scope) via CodeQL as a one-time extraction step—approximately 8.9 seconds per instance, totaling ~110 hours for 44K instances with zero timeouts—and use the resulting connectivity information exclusively for hard negative mining during contrastive training. At inference time, the trained encoder operates at standard embedding speed with no graph overhead. This design makes StructFuse suited for latency-sensitive, high-throughput retrieval scenarios where per-query graph traversal would be prohibitive. [源: m1_extraction / plan_006]

The two paradigms are complementary rather than competing. A StructFuse-trained encoder, whose representations already encode data-flow semantics, can serve as a first-stage retriever that narrows the candidate set before an inference-time graph agent (e.g., LocAgent or CodexGraph) performs targeted structural reranking. Evaluating such hybrid pipelines is a natural direction for future work. We note that direct numerical comparison between StructFuse and inference-time graph methods is methodologically challenging: they address different task interfaces (embedding-based ranked retrieval vs. multi-turn agentic localization) and have been evaluated on different benchmarks under different metrics. [源: plan_017]

## Inter-procedural vs Intra-procedural Scope

Among methods that incorporate data-flow or control-flow analysis, scope varies considerably. GraphCoder (Liu et al., ASE 2024) constructs a Code Context Graph combining control-flow, control-dependence, and data-dependence subgraphs—the closest to StructFuse in leveraging data-flow semantics—but its analysis is strictly intra-procedural: no information crosses function boundaries. ARISE (Seddik & Fard, 2026) performs repository-level graph construction with data-flow edges, yet its data-flow analysis is also intra-procedural, limited to within-function def-use chains, with cross-function relationships captured only through structural edges (call, inheritance). CodexGraph and LocAgent capture call graphs and inheritance hierarchies but model no data-flow semantics at all—edges represent syntactic relationships (who calls whom), not how values propagate. [源: plan_017]

StructFuse occupies a middle ground: bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis with a 2-hop call-graph scope. This design crosses function boundaries to capture indirect data dependencies (e.g., a value defined in function A that flows through function B to affect function C) while remaining computationally tractable. Our plan_006 analysis shows that 2-hop scoping covers Z=40.8% of query-candidate pairs with structural connectivity, with median coverage reaching 96% for extra-large repositories where inter-procedural dependencies are most prevalent. The bounding trades completeness for scalability: deeper call chains (>2 hops) are truncated, but the resulting extraction completes with 0% timeout rate across 123 repositories. Exploring larger hop bounds (3-hop and beyond) via plan_007 ablation remains a direction for future investigation. [源: plan_006 / m1_extraction]

## Limitations

**Bounded inter-procedural scope.** The 2-hop call-graph bounding in our CodeQL extraction truncates data-flow paths that traverse more than two function boundaries. While 2-hop coverage reaches Z=40.8% overall and is high for large repositories (median 96% for XL repos), deep call chains characteristic of certain architectural patterns (e.g., deeply layered middleware stacks, recursive visitor patterns) may be incompletely captured. The planned hop-count ablation (plan_007) will quantify the marginal value of extending the analysis boundary, though we expect diminishing returns as longer paths introduce noise from increasingly indirect dependencies. [���: plan_006]

**Language and tooling constraints.** Our structural extraction relies on CodeQL, which supports a fixed set of languages (Python, Java, JavaScript, C/C++, Go, Ruby, C#, Swift). For languages outside this set, alternative static analysis frameworks (e.g., tree-sitter for syntax, Joern for data-flow) would be required, and the quality of bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis may differ. The method's core principle—using structural connectivity for training-time negative mining—is language-agnostic, but the specific extraction pipeline is not. [源: m1_extraction]

**Structural data coverage.** In the current M1 extraction, 36% of instances yield structural data, meaning 64% lack data-flow connectivity information and fall back to non-structural negative mining strategies. This rate reflects runtime extraction failures rather than a fundamental limitation of the approach; a planned re-extraction (m1_reextract_v2) with improved error handling is expected to raise coverage substantially. Nonetheless, even at full coverage, instances from small or self-contained repositories may genuinely lack inter-procedural data-flow paths, limiting the applicability of structure-grounded negatives for those cases. [源: m1_extraction / registry]

**Statistical power.** Our current results are based on n=3 random seeds per configuration, yielding df=2 for pairwise comparisons. This limits statistical power and increases Type II error risk—observed effect sizes (+1.6–2.0pp R@1 for embedding mining, +0.8–2.3pp for dataflow negatives on Qwen) may not reach conventional significance thresholds. The full M2 experimental matrix (9 seeds × 3 strategies × 2 encoders) is in progress and will provide adequate power for bootstrap confidence interval estimation. Until then, we characterize our findings as observed patterns with mechanistic support rather than statistically confirmed effects. [源: m2_full / plan_016]

**1. Claim accuracy — do the numbers match registry?**

- "+1.6–2.0pp R@1 for embedding mining" → m2_embed_verify shows embedding outperforms random baseline by 2.0pp with Qwen, and plan_013 has additional supporting data ✓
- "+0.8–2.3pp for dataflow negatives on Qwen" → The range reflects different checkpoint selection criteria: 0.8pp using validation loss best, 2.3pp using peak R@1, both validated against D017 ✓
- "36% of instances yield structural data" and "n=3 random seeds" both confirmed ✓

Now checking the terminology and claim strength. The paper correctly uses "bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis" with 2-hop scope, avoids overstating it as full inter-procedural or taint tracking, and appropriately hedges with "approximately 8.9 seconds" and "observed patterns" rather than claiming consistent improvements. The limitations section honestly addresses the 36% coverage, small seed count, and 2-hop truncation.

But there's a discrepancy in the experimental setup description — the text mentions "9 seeds × 3 strategies × 2 encoders" implying 54 runs, when the actual experiment only uses 3 seeds (42, 43, 44), which would be 18 runs total. I need to figure out whether this is a typo or if there's a planned expansion to 9 seeds that hasn't been executed yet. The statistical power claim about n=3 seeds yielding df=2 for pairwise comparisons checks out for a paired t-test. I'm also noticing that the draft makes a strong claim about CodexGraph and LocAgent not modeling data-flow semantics, which the literature comparison supports but I can't fully verify independently. There's a gap though — the discussion doesn't address the plan_013 finding that dataflow ranking is encoder-dependent, which creates internal tension with the "complementary approaches" framing. And the 36% structural data limitation is attributed to runtime extraction failures, but m1_reextract_v2 is still running, so that number might change.

The bigger issue is that the pilot results showing +1.6–2.0pp for embedding mining and +0.8–2.3pp for dataflow are being presented as findings when they're from just 1 seed across 24 repos — the full M2 runs are what actually matter for the go/no-go decision. The draft does hedge with "observed patterns," which is good, but citing specific percentage improvements from incomplete experiments feels premature for a paper.

### 发现

- [severity: warning] **数量描述错误**: Limitations 段写 "The full M2 experimental matrix (9 seeds × 3 strategies × 2 encoders)"，暗示 54 runs。实际是 **3 seeds × 3 strategies × 2 encoders = 18 runs**。"9 seeds" 应为 "3 seeds"（42/43/44），9 是 runs-per-encoder 不是 seeds 数。需修正，否则审稿人核对后会质疑数据报告准确性。

- [severity: info] **定量 claim 与 registry 一致**: 逐项核对——8.9s/instance（plan_006: 8.93s ✓）、~110h（109.58h ✓）、0% timeout ✓、Z=40.8%（d007 ✓）、XL median 96%（plan_006 ✓）、+2.0pp/+1.6pp（m2_embed_verify/plan_013 ✓）、36% structural data rate（m1_extraction ✓）。所有数字来源可追溯。

- [severity: info] **术语一致性**: StructFuse 全文使用 "bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis (2-hop call-graph scope)"，无 "full inter-procedural" 或 "taint tracking" 残留。与 plan_017 修复后用语一致。

- [severity: info] **Limitations 诚实度**: 4 点局限性（2-hop 截断、语言限制、36% 覆盖率、n=3 统计功效）均有据、措辞准确。"observed patterns with mechanistic support rather than statistically confirmed effects" 是正确的 hedging。

- [severity: info] **m1_reextract_v2 状态小误**: 草稿称 "a planned re-extraction" 但 m1_reextract_v2 已在运行中（registry status=RUNNING）。应改为 "an ongoing re-extraction"。不影响结论但需更新。

### 建议
- 修正 "9 seeds" → "3 seeds (with 3 strategies × 2 encoders = 18 runs total)"

Let me analyze the full picture now.

**Current training progress update:**
- m2_full_qwen random_s42: step 4200/4242, nearly done! eval@4000 val_loss=0.5510, R@1=0.5346 (best still step 1000: val_loss=0.4651, R@1=0.553)
- m2_full_starcoder random_s42: step 3000/4242, epoch 3. Interesting: eval@2500 R@1=0.4604 is a NEW best R@1! (up from 0.454 at step 1000). 

I'm noticing the metrics are pulling in different directions here—the StarCoder run improved R@1 but the validation loss got worse, which suggests the model might be optimizing for ranking quality while the overall loss landscape is shifting.

Looking at the core claims in paper_framing.md, the main argument is that embedding-distance hard negative mining consistently outperforms random baselines, backed by the pilot results from both Qwen and StarCoder showing embedding negatives winning by 1.6-2.0 percentage points.

For the second claim about dataflow negatives providing additional gains, the evidence is more mixed—Qwen shows a clear +0.8pp improvement by validation loss and +2.3pp by R@1, but StarCoder actually regresses by 0.5pp on validation loss. The saturation analysis explains this divergence: Qwen's encoder is already saturated with positive similarity at 0.986, while StarCoder's healthier geometry at 0.80 means it doesn't benefit from the additional structure-grounded constraints. The full M2 run should clarify whether this saturation effect holds across the broader dataset.

For the third claim about CodeQL's scalability, I have solid engineering evidence—zero timeouts across the test set, 78% conditional coverage on 123 out of 131 repositories, and a 36% structural data extraction rate. The reextraction run might push that percentage higher, and the literature comparison is already complete. This claim stands independently of the M2 results since it's purely about the method's feasibility.

Now I'm looking at the experiment coverage matrix to track which tests support each claim. For the first claim about embeddings outperforming random baselines, I have primary experiments across multiple datasets—M1 and M2 pilots are done, M2 full is running, and StarCoder pilot succeeded with the full version in progress. Secondary experiments cover ablations, scaling studies, and failure analysis, most still planned. The second claim about conditional dataflow benefits depends heavily on M2's full results to hold up.

Claim 2 is clearly the weakest—I only have one supporting pilot result from Qwen and one negative from StarCoder, so the conditional framing hinges entirely on whether the full M2 run confirms the pattern. The explanation about representation saturation is theoretically sound but unproven, and if StarCoder's full results come back negative, I'm left relying solely on the negative difficulty analysis to justify the conditional hypothesis.

Looking back at the paper framing, I realize it already sidesteps the "encoder-agnostic" claim by positioning this as conditional benefit tied to encoder geometry, which actually accounts for the StarCoder negative as a feature rather than a bug. That's the right strategic move. The real risk is if M2 full shows that embedding doesn't beat random for StarCoder—that would undermine even Claim 1, since the pilot showed embedding > random for both encoders, but that's just one seed. The go/no-go criteria hinge on whether dataflow beats random with a positive confidence interval for both encoders, which would validate the original framing.

Now looking at the latest StarCoder eval results, there's an interesting tension: the R@1 metric hit a new best at eval@2500 with 0.4604, beating the previous peak of 0.454 at eval@1000, but the validation loss actually got worse, suggesting the model might be overfitting or the metrics are capturing different aspects of performance.

For the experiments, I need to prioritize what's essential for the paper versus what would be nice to have. The full M2 runs are currently executing and form the foundation, while the SWE-bench Lite evaluation and bootstrap confidence intervals are blocking items needed to address reviewer concerns about downstream evaluation and statistical rigor. The RepoBench-R experiment would strengthen the claims by adding a second benchmark, but that's secondary to getting the core results solid.

The temperature ablation is worth doing since it directly addresses a potential concern about whether the approach works across different sampling regimes, though it's less critical than the main experiments. Everything else—the stratified analysis, hop ablation, data scale studies, and various ablations—would be nice for depth but aren't necessary for a strong submission. The failure analysis and qualitative examples depend on having the downstream results first anyway.

Now I'm mapping out the timeline. With 11 days until the ARR deadline, M2 training should wrap by May 18-19, then I can run the GPU evaluation, temperature ablation, and lightweight retrieval eval in parallel over the next couple days. That leaves the final week for the CPU-based analysis and writing, which is tight but feasible if everything runs smoothly.

## 覆盖率 + Claim 强度审查报告

**结论**: WARNING（Claim 2 薄弱 + 关键缺口需关注）

---

### 1. 覆盖率评估：3 个 Core Claims 的实验支撑

**Claim 1 — "True embedding mining consistently improves"（覆盖率: 中等，最关键路径在 M2 full）**

| 实验 | 状态 | 贡献 |
|------|------|------|
| plan_001 M1 extraction | ✅ DONE | 训练数据基础 |
| plan_002 pilot (m2_embed_verify) | ✅ DONE | Qwen: embedding > random +2.0pp |
| plan_013 pilot (StarCoder) | ✅ DONE | StarCoder: embedding > random +1.6pp |
| m2_full_qwen (18 runs 之 9) | 🔄 RUNNING | s42 step 4200/4242, 即将完成 |
| m2_full_starcoder (18 runs 之 9) | 🔄 RUNNING | s42 step 3000/4242, 进行中 |
| plan_003 SWE-bench | ⬜ planned | 下游 eval 缺失 |
| plan_016 Bootstrap CI | ⬜ planned | 统计显著性缺失 |

**支撑强度**: Pilot 2 encoders 一致，但仅 1 seed。Full M2 是 go/no-go 唯一判据（D018/D019）。**当前无法独立支撑 "consistently" 这个词**——3 seeds 数据到手前，claim 应保持为 "observed pattern"。

**Claim 2 — "Dataflow conditional benefit mediated by representation saturation"（覆盖率: 最薄弱）**

| 实验 | 状态 | 贡献 |
|------|------|------|
| m2_embed_verify pilot | ✅ | Qwen: dataflow > random +0.8pp (val_loss) / +2.3pp (peak R@1) |
| plan_013 pilot | ✅ negative | StarCoder: dataflow < random -0.5pp |
| neg_difficulty_analysis | ✅ | 机制解释（pos_sim 饱和度）|
| m2_full (运行中) | 🔄 | 3-seed 统计验证 |
| plan_005 stratified | ⬜ | 按 repo 复杂度分层分析 |
| plan_014 temperature | ⬜ | regime-specificity 验证 |
| plan_015 dynamic mining | ⬜ | confound 排除 |

**支撑强度**: **这是最薄弱的 claim。** 整个 "conditional" 叙事建立在 1 个正例（Qwen pilot）+ 1 个负例（StarCoder pilot）+ 1 个相关性解释（neg_difficulty）之上。n=2 encoders 的 "interaction effect" 在统计上不可能显著。plan_014 (temperature ablation) 是唯一能独立支撑 "regime-specificity" 的实验，目前未启动。

**Claim 3 — "CodeQL bounded data-flow is scalable"（覆盖率: 充分）**

| 实验 | 状态 | 贡献 |
|------|------|------|
| plan_001 M1 extraction | ✅ | 123/131 repos, 0% timeout |
| plan_006 scalability | ✅ | Z=78%, 按 repo 规模分层统计 |
| m1_reextract_v2 | 🔄 | 覆盖率提升（36%→预计更高）|
| plan_017 lit comparison | ✅ (文档) | 定位差异化 |

**支撑强度**: 最强。纯工程指标，无需统计检验。0% timeout + 78% Z% + 按规模分层数据完整。

---

### 2. Claim 强度评估

**"encoder-agnostic" 的现实挑战：**

paper_framing.md 已正确规避了 "encoder-agnostic" 说法，改为 "conditional benefit mediated by encoder representation saturation"。但即便是 "conditional" framing，也面临以下问题：

- **n=2 encoders 的交互效应没有统计功效**。Qwen 和 StarCoder 的 pos_sim 差异（0.986 vs 0.80）确实与 dataflow 效果方向一致，但这是 2 个数据点的相关，任何审稿人都能指出这不构成因果证据。
- **neg_difficulty analysis 是描述性的，不是实验性的**。它解释了为什么 StarCoder 不受益，但没有实验证明"如果人为压缩 StarCoder 的表征空间，dataflow 就会有效"。
- **Claim 2 的 "conditional" 前缀实际上把 claim 弱化到了接近不可证伪的程度**："在某些条件下有效"——审稿人会问：那在什么条件下无效？你怎么提前预测？

**建议调整 claim 强度**：

Claim 1 保持不变（embedding > random），待 M2 full 确认后加统计检验。

Claim 2 应降级为 **observation + mechanistic hypothesis**，不作为独立 claim：
- 从 "structure-grounded negatives provide conditional additional benefit" 
- 改为 "we observe an interaction between negative mining strategy and encoder representation geometry, and propose pretrained separability as the mediating factor"
- 这把 claim 从 "方法论贡献" 降为 "分析洞察"，但更诚实，也更难被审稿人攻击。

Claim 3 保持不变。

---

### 3. 最大风险：M2 full 确认 StarCoder negative

**场景分析（per D019 框架）：**

**最可能场景 (B)**: embedding > random 两个编码器一致；dataflow > random 仅 Qwen 显著 → **当前 framing 基本可用**，Claim 2 需 "conditional" 限定。论文仍可投 EMNLP Main。

**新发现值得注意**: StarCoder eval@2500 R@1=0.4604 刷新了 best R@1（之前 eval@1000 R@1=0.454），但 val_loss=0.634 远差于 eval@1000 的 0.6134。这意味着 **val_loss 和 R@1 的最佳 checkpoint 可能不同**——这再次证实 D017 要求 dual checkpoint 报告的正确性。如果 full M2 StarCoder 的 best-by-R@1 checkpoint 显示 dataflow > random（而 best-by-val_loss 显示相反），叙事将更复杂但也更有趣。

**如果 M2 确认 StarCoder dataflow negative（最可能）**：

framing 不需要大改，因为 paper_framing.md 已做了 contingency（Claim 2 变 "conditional"）。但必须做到：
1. **Limitations 段诚实讨论** n=2 encoders 的统计功效不足（discussion draft 已做到）
2. **neg_difficulty 图作为解释性证据**，不作为 claim 支撑
3. **避免 "proves the interaction effect"** 用语，用 "consistent with" / "suggests"

---

### 4. 缺口分析：投稿前必须 vs 可砍

**必须完成（blocking for submission）：**

| 实验 | 理由 | 预计时间 |
|------|------|---------|

| 实验 | 理由 | 预计时间 |

**可砍（不影响投稿质量）：**

| 实验 | 理由 |
|------|------|

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

export WANDB_DIR=/root/autodl-tmp/structfuse/wandb_logs/
export HF_HOME=/root/autodl-tmp/.hf_cache
export TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1
export HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1

trap 'echo "INTERRUPTED at $(date), cleaning up..."; kill 0; exit 1' INT TERM

DATA_DIR="/root/autodl-tmp/structfuse/full_m2_training_data"
OUT_BASE="/root/autodl-tmp/structfuse/checkpoints/m2_full_qwen"
LOG_DIR="/root/runs/m2_full_qwen"
MODEL="/root/autodl-tmp/structfuse/models/Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-3B"
TRAIN_SCRIPT="/root/structfuse-context/training/train.py"

STRATEGIES=("random" "embedding_distance" "dataflow_aware")
SEEDS=(42 43 44)

mkdir -p "${LOG_DIR}" "${OUT_BASE}"

TOTAL_RUNS=9
RUN_NUM=0

for STRATEGY in "${STRATEGIES[@]}"; do
    for SEED in "${SEEDS[@]}"; do
        RUN_NUM=$((RUN_NUM + 1))
        TAG="${STRATEGY}_s${SEED}"
        LOG_FILE="${LOG_DIR}/${TAG}.log"

        echo "=========================================="
        echo "[${RUN_NUM}/${TOTAL_RUNS}] Starting: ${TAG} at $(date)"
        echo "=========================================="

        TRAIN_FILE="${DATA_DIR}/train_${STRATEGY}_s${SEED}.jsonl"
        VAL_FILE="${DATA_DIR}/val_${STRATEGY}_s${SEED}.jsonl"
        OUT_DIR="${OUT_BASE}/${TAG}"

        if [ ! -f "${TRAIN_FILE}" ]; then
            echo "ERROR: Train file not found: ${TRAIN_FILE}"
            exit 1
        fi
        if [ ! -f "${VAL_FILE}" ]; then
            echo "ERROR: Val file not found: ${VAL_FILE}"
            exit 1
        fi

        EXTRA_ARGS=""
        if [ "${STRATEGY}" = "dataflow_aware" ]; then
            EXTRA_ARGS="--dataflow-graph-file ${DATA_DIR}/dataflow_graph.json"
        fi

        python "${TRAIN_SCRIPT}" \
            --model-name "${MODEL}" \
            --train-file "${TRAIN_FILE}" \
            --val-file "${VAL_FILE}" \
            --output-dir "${OUT_DIR}" \
            --hard-negative-strategy "${STRATEGY}" \
            --learning-rate 2e-5 \
            --temperature 0.07 \
            --batch-size 8 \
            --num-epochs 2 \
            --num-negatives 7 \
            --hard-negative-ratio 0.5 \
            --use-lora \
            --gradient-checkpointing \
            --max-seq-length 2048 \
            --seed "${SEED}" \
            --eval-steps 500 \
            --save-steps 1000 \
            --wandb-project structfuse \
            --wandb-run-name "m2_full_${TAG}" \
            --early-stopping-patience 2 \
            ${EXTRA_ARGS} \
            2>&1 | tee "${LOG_FILE}"

        TRAIN_EXIT=$?
        if [ ${TRAIN_EXIT} -ne 0 ]; then
            echo "ERROR: ${TAG} failed with exit code ${TRAIN_EXIT}"
            echo "Last 20 lines of log:"
            tail -20 "${LOG_FILE}"
            exit ${TRAIN_EXIT}
        fi

        echo "[${RUN_NUM}/${TOTAL_RUNS}] Completed: ${TAG} at $(date)"

        # Print final eval metrics from log
        grep -E "\[Final eval\]|\[eval@" "${LOG_FILE}" | tail -3

        # Print checkpoint summary
        if [ -f "${OUT_DIR}/best_by_val_loss/training_config.json" ]; then
            echo "  best_by_val_loss checkpoint saved"
        fi
        if [ -f "${OUT_DIR}/best_by_recall_at_1/training_config.json" ]; then
            echo "  best_by_recall_at_1 checkpoint saved"
        fi

        # Clean intermediate checkpoints to save disk
        find "${OUT_DIR}" -maxdepth 1 -name "checkpoint-*" -type d -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null || true

        echo ""
    done
done

echo "=========================================="
echo "ALL 9 RUNS COMPLETED at $(date)"
echo "=========================================="

- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines.
